purpose: Metformin is used to help control blood sugar levels in people with type 2 diabetes. It is often one of the first medicines doctors prescribe when someone is diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. It can also help lower the risk of serious diabetes complications like heart disease and kidney problems.
how_it_works: Metformin works in a few helpful ways to keep your blood sugar from getting too high. It tells your liver to slow down and stop releasing extra sugar into your blood. It also helps your body use insulin more effectively, so sugar can move out of your blood and into your cells where it belongs.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects are stomach-related and include nausea, diarrhea, stomach upset, or a metallic taste in your mouth. These usually happen when you first start taking it and often get better after a few weeks. Taking it with food can help reduce these stomach problems.
warnings: A rare but serious condition called lactic acidosis can occur, so contact your doctor right away if you feel very weak, have unusual muscle pain, trouble breathing, or stomach discomfort. Tell your doctor if you drink a lot of alcohol, have kidney problems, or are scheduled for surgery or an imaging scan with contrast dye, as you may need to temporarily stop this medication. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first.
typical_dosing: Metformin is usually started at a low dose, such as 500 mg once or twice a day with meals, to help your stomach adjust. Your doctor may slowly increase your dose over several weeks up to a maximum of 2,550 mg per day. The extended-release version is taken once a day with your evening meal.
